title: Most Readers Say Flying Cars Are Not Ready to Take Off Yet
summary:
Are flying cars almost here, or are they still just a dream? Readers of Live Science have strong opinions, and most are not holding their breath.

The debate restarted last week, when Tesla demonstrated a new "flying" edition of its Roadster electric vehicle, called the Rocket Roadster. Some experts remain skeptical it is feasible, but the demonstration reignited a long-standing argument about flying cars.

In response, Live Science asked readers whether flying cars will be available in the next five years. More than 280 responded. The largest group, 34 percent, chose "No, we need more than five years for flying cars to take off." Next, 23 percent chose "No, flying cars will never happen."

Many comments explained that doubt. One reader, drawing on almost 60 years of driving experience, wrote that most people cannot handle driving in two dimensions, let alone three. The same reader also pointed to hunger, poverty, inadequate healthcare, and disregard for the planet, and asked what we are leaving future generations.

Another reader was just as doubtful, arguing a flying car would never become a cheap alternative to ordinary vehicles. Gravity rules on this planet, the reader argued, and imagining ordinary people flying above towns, suburbs, cities, and parks raised worries about damage and protests.

Not everyone was so negative. Another commenter praised Tesla's technology, pointing to the Roadster, the Tesla Y, the Cybercab, and Starship as at the frontier of science. The same reader argued that Tesla's founder has revolutionized cars and space travel in under 20 years, noting that the first Tesla car was sold in 2008.

The poll does not settle the question. It shows a public that is curious, but mostly cautious. For now, flying cars remain a demonstration and a debate, not something you can buy and fly home.
why_it_matters: How people judge new technology matters beyond cars, because safety, cost, and shared skies affect everyone who lives under them.

background_read: A flying car is a vehicle meant to travel on roads and also fly through the air.
Flying adds a third direction, up and down, to the usual forward, backward, left, and right of driving.
That raises practical questions about safety, cost, rules for the sky, and what happens above homes and parks.
A demonstration shows an idea in action, but it does not by itself mean the vehicle is ready for everyone to buy and use.
